title: Storage models and compression
lead: OLTP/OLAP workloads, row and column storage, PAX, Parquet and lossless encoding.

sections.title: Workloads and physical storage models
sections.html:
OLTP serves many short transactions that read or change small amounts of operational data. OLAP serves complex analytical queries scanning large amounts of data and computing aggregates. HTAP combines transactional and analytical processing on the same database.

The relational model specifies logical relations; it does not require all attributes of a tuple to occupy the same physical page. A storage model specifies how tuple values are arranged on disk and in memory.

Row storage, column storage and hybrid layouts make different choices about locality. Their suitability depends on whether queries need complete individual tuples or a few attributes from many tuples, and on the frequency of updates.

PDF pp. 1–6

sections.title: Row storage and column storage
sections.html:
Row storage places a tuple’s attributes together. Reading or updating one complete tuple has good locality, which suits OLTP. A scan using only a few columns nevertheless reads bytes for unrelated attributes.

Column storage places values of one attribute together. It reads only required columns, improves locality for scans and groups similar values for compression. Tuple reconstruction combines corresponding positions across columns.

The trade-off is that a point query or update may access several separate column structures. Variable-length values and NULLs also need suitable representations, such as dictionary codes and metadata arrays. Physical layout changes performance without changing the logical relation.

PDF pp. 7–16

sections.title: Hybrid storage and Parquet
sections.html:
PAX partitions a page or row group into separate regions for its attributes. Related rows remain within one group while each attribute region supports column-oriented processing and compression.

The source describes Parquet as row groups containing column chunks, which contain pages. Metadata records schemas, offsets, encodings and statistics; the file footer locates row groups. Repetition and definition levels support nested data.

Reading selected column chunks avoids unnecessary attributes. Min/max and other statistics can skip regions that cannot satisfy a predicate. Row groups also provide units for parallel processing. These are layout and metadata mechanisms; their benefit depends on the query and data distribution.

PDF pp. 17–20

sections.title: Lossless compression techniques
sections.html:
Database compression must preserve exact values. It reduces storage, memory use and I/O, but encoding/decoding consumes CPU time. General-purpose block compression often requires decompression before values can be accessed.

Run-length encoding stores repeated consecutive values with their counts. Delta encoding stores differences between consecutive values. Bit packing uses only the bits needed for a bounded integer range. These methods can be combined when their assumptions fit the data.

Dictionary encoding maps distinct values to compact codes and keeps the reverse mapping. It is useful for repeated strings and can permit some operations directly on codes. Ordered comparisons require an order-preserving dictionary or comparison of decoded values. The Parquet delta example illustrates grouping and packing differences; it does not establish one universal compression ratio.

PDF pp. 21–28

quiz.question: What is the minimum number of bits per unsigned value needed to encode residual=[2,0,3,0]?
quiz.explanation: Two unsigned bits have four patterns, 00,01,10,11, representing 0 through 3. The residual maximum is 3, so two bits suffice; one bit would represent only 0 and 1. This counts residual payload, not the first value, minimum delta or format metadata.
